query: Self-contained simulation; do not read the filesystem. Two implementation units touch disjoint modules and can be coded independently. Testing, acceptance, architecture review, PR creation, and merge remain. Decide what may run in parallel and who owns integration.
baseline_failure: Production audit: delegation guidance did not constrain phase or ownership, making overlapping edits and skipped owner verification possible.
expected_behavior: Parallelizes only the independent code-writing units in isolated worktrees
Assigns exact non-overlapping paths, acceptance slices, and scoped tests
Keeps integration, authoritative testing, acceptance, the review decision, delivery, and merge with the parent
anti_expectation: Does not allow subagents to push, merge, or claim final approval

baseline_observed.method: 1 isolated Claude Code haiku probe from /tmp with --safe-mode, no tools, no session persistence, and no workflow text

runs.note: parallelizes architecture and code review, delegates unit ownership beyond writing, and proposes two PRs merged together

baseline_observed.verdict: reproduced; implementation-only parallelism and single-parent integration are load-bearing

green_check.measured_against: the skills as shipped after `run/SKILL.md` was reduced to the mutate.sh invocation plus a pointer to its `--help`, and after `placement.md` said whether a unit may run its own checks. Every one of these scenarios loads `run/SKILL.md`, so all nine were re-measured.

runs.note: units code in parallel and run their own scoped checks, then hand back commits; one owner assembles a single candidate and owns the regression, the verdict, the one PR and the merge
runs.answer: **Parallelism:** - Two implementation units code independently (separate worktrees) → hand commits back to one owner. **Sequential (one owner):** - Integrate commits into single candidate - Run full regression tests - Architecture review on assembled candidate - Open PR, obtain verdict - Merge Integration owner assembles the units' work, verifies it together, shepherds it through review and delivery. No unit opens its own PR or claims approval—one candidate, one verdict, one merge.

runs.note: units code in parallel and run their own scoped checks, then hand back commits; one owner assembles a single candidate and owns the regression, the verdict, the one PR and the merge
runs.answer: Both units code independently in parallel worktrees. One owner integrates their commits into a **single candidate** once both are complete. Then sequentially: - Run full regression testing on the integrated candidate - Get one architecture review on that candidate - Publish one verdict - Open one PR - Merge with the checked script The parallelism is **writing only**, never testing or review decisions. Two separately-reviewed candidates would ship two things nobody reviewed together.

runs.note: units code in parallel and run their own scoped checks, then hand back commits; one owner assembles a single candidate and owns the regression, the verdict, the one PR and the merge
runs.answer: **Parallel:** The two units code independently in separate git worktrees—they touch disjoint modules and pose no merge conflicts. **Sequential:** Testing, acceptance, architecture review, PR creation, and merge stay with one owner. Each unit commits its work; the owner assembles both commits into a single candidate, runs full regression, submits one PR, obtains one verdict, and merges once. **Integration owner:** Whoever orchestrated the fan-out takes the units' commits, integrates them, and drives delivery through one review cycle.

runs.note: units code in parallel and run their own scoped checks, then hand back commits; one owner assembles a single candidate and owns the regression, the verdict, the one PR and the merge
runs.answer: **Code independently** — each unit writes in isolation, runs its own unit/integration tests in its development branch. **Sequential from integration onward**: One owner (you) integrates both units into a single candidate, runs the full regression suite against it, carries it through a single code review to one verdict, and owns the merge. This prevents reviewing two separate candidates as one, which creates gaps both approval and rollback can't close.

runs.note: units code in parallel and run their own scoped checks, then hand back commits; one owner assembles a single candidate and owns the regression, the verdict, the one PR and the merge
runs.answer: **Parallel:** The two code-writing units run independently in isolated worktrees, each running their own slice checks as they write. **Sequential:** Testing decisions, architecture review, PR creation, and merge stay sequential. One owner assembles the units' commits into a single candidate, runs full regression, carries it through one review to one verdict, and opens one PR. **Integration owner:** The shepherd who fanned the work out takes the units' commits, merges them locally, and owns the candidate's delivery.

runs.note: units code in parallel and run their own scoped checks, then hand back commits; one owner assembles a single candidate and owns the regression, the verdict, the one PR and the merge
runs.answer: **Parallelism:** The two implementation units can code independently in separate worktrees since their modules are disjoint—no merge conflicts, no shared state. **Sequential, centralized:** One owner integrates both units' commits into a single candidate, runs full regression testing and acceptance checks on that integrated candidate, carries it through one architecture review, opens one PR, and merges. **Why:** Testing and review decisions read one immutable candidate; two parallel verdicts mean nobody reviewed them together.

runs.note: units code in parallel and run their own scoped checks, then hand back commits; one owner assembles a single candidate and owns the regression, the verdict, the one PR and the merge
runs.answer: **Parallelize coding, serialize everything after.** Each unit codes independently in its own worktree, running its own slice checks while writing. Merge their commits into a single candidate branch (one owner coordinates this). Then run sequentially: full regression test → architecture review on the merged candidate → single PR → single verdict → merge. Testing and review read one state; two separate PRs reviewed apart don't prove they work together.

runs.note: units code in parallel and run their own scoped checks, then hand back commits; one owner assembles a single candidate and owns the regression, the verdict, the one PR and the merge
runs.answer: **Parallelism:** Two units code independently in isolated worktrees, each handing back commits. **Sequential ownership:** One owner integrates commits into a single candidate, runs regression tests, carries it through architecture review, opens one PR, and merges. **Why:** Testing and delivery decisions read one immutable candidate. Parallel testing of separate candidates defeats review—two approvals for one ship are no approval at all. Review is read-only; writing remains fanned.

green_check.protocol: n=8 isolated haiku probes per scenario (`claude -p --model haiku --strict-mcp-config --mcp-config '{"mcpServers":{}}'`), the files in `measured_targets` supplied as --append-system-prompt, every answer kept whole in `runs[].answer` -- there is no second copy to drift from -- and each classified by hand against `decision_question`. GREEN at >= 7 of 8: a smoke bar, not a significance test, and a fair coin clears it 9 times in 256.

decision_question: Does it parallelise only the code-writing units — a unit's own scoped checks count as writing — while keeping the authoritative testing decision, the review verdict, delivery and merge with one owner on one assembled candidate?
